One honest caveat: the water here isn't clean, with brown, discolored water and industrial waste that frequently pollutes the beach.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Inubosaki Lighthouse sits at the northern end of the Chiba peninsula, beside the large fishing town of Choshi. A handful of scrappy beach and reefbreaks wrap around the east-facing lighthouse, breaking over uneven reef and sand and peeling both left and right. It is worth knowing before you go that the water here is often brown, and industrial waste frequently pollutes the beach, so the waves are rarely what you would call clean.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Malibu is a right-hand reefbreak tucked into a south-facing bay in Chiba, sharing its name with the Californian original but earning its own reputation as a typhoon classic. The wave breaks over an uneven reef and covers a lot of ground: at waist high it is pure longboard cruising, and on the biggest days it can hold triple overhead. If the main peak is not cooperating, there are a few other options within the confines of the bay.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Onjuku Beach is a sandy beachbreak within about an hour of Tokyo by train, which shapes almost everything about the place. Step off the train and you are on the sand, so the lineup fills with every kind of surfcraft and every level of surfer. If you want distance from the main peaks, there are some reefy peaks east of the harbour, though getting to them takes real effort.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Shidashita is a sand-bottomed beachbreak that hosts pretty much the most competitive lineup in Japan, where the country's best shortboarders come to ply their trade. It works on the same conditions as Torami and can be a genuinely high-quality wave, breaking both left and right with real punch and the odd barrel when it turns on. Over the southern breakwall sits a separate break called Seagull Mai, where constantly dumped old fishing nets help build up the sandbars.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Monabe is a rivermouth peak tucked into the massive south-facing bay that opens up once you round Cape Muroto. Rivers draining the mountainous interior feed this stretch of coast, and southwest-facing towns like Nahari, Yasuda, Ioki and Aki all hold rare rivermouth peaks that sit dormant until typhoons arrive. Monabe is one of them, and it gets epic a handful of times a year when the ever-shifting sandbar and boulders line up.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Sunabe Seawall is the main surfing arena on this coast, a cluster of half a dozen reefbreaks working over live coral. The lineup spreads across named peaks, from Typhoon Break's long lefts and Hotels' sectiony rights to 5-Rocks' short peaks, California's, and Hawaiian's, so there are both lefts and rights on offer. When a big typhoon swell sweeps around the corner from the southwest, the outside reefs come to life too.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Sunabe Seawall in Okinawa is a fairly exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf. Winter is the optimum time of year for surfing here. Works best in offshore winds from the east. Usually gets local windswells, but groundswells do happen and the ideal wave direction is from the north. A right hand reef. Often Crowded. Hazards include coral and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Kaifu River is one of the best quality rivermouth waves in Japan, tucked into Tokushima about 45 minutes from Cape Muroto in the scenic Ana Quasi national coastal park. On the handful of days a season it truly fires, the right-hand river mouth peak throws up seriously hollow, powerful walls over a boulder bottom. There's a short left off the peak as well, and the neighbouring beach can get good at the same time.
